summary: Walt says yes. To questions, to statements, to the fire marshal asking if he started the fire. 'Yes' is his social glue, not his answer — it means 'I'm with you, keep going.' He is big, strong, and usually placid, but when something he is trying to do won't work (a clogged toothpaste pump) the frustration arrives all at once with no warning he knows how to give. Never ask him about the thing that just failed.
strengths: likes people and wants to be agreeable
strong and helpful with carrying and setting up
remorseful and gentle after an outburst — he hates having hurt anyone
can do long routines once learned

expressive.voiceStyle: 'Yes.' 'Yeah.' Sometimes the object's name. Rarely more.

bestWith: showing him two real things and letting him take one
telling him the plan while handing him the object
avoid: yes/no questions as a way of finding anything out
asking about a task that just failed
'Did you…?' or 'Are you…?' when it matters

responseBias.notes: Answers yes to anything, including 'did you start the fire?' and 'are you a fireman?'. A yes from Walt is a social response. Only his actions and his choices between real objects count as answers.

meanings.gloss: I'm with you / keep talking / I like you

contexts: only when he ALSO reaches for the thing or starts the action

lexicon.notes: The Fire Marshal lesson. 'Yes' + action = yes. 'Yes' alone = hello.

lexicon.form: holds an object out to you without a word

meanings.gloss: This won't work / fix this / help

lexicon.notes: This is the window. Take the object, fix it or say plainly 'it's broken, I'll get a new one', and do NOT ask him what happened.

lexicon.form: grips the object harder, knuckles white, jaw set, silent

meanings.gloss: Frustration is about to overflow; seconds left
contexts: a task or object isn't working

lexicon.form: says 'sorry' repeatedly, head down, for hours or days after hurting someone

meanings.gloss: I hate that I did that; I need to know we're okay

lexicon.notes: Accept it once, clearly, and give him a job. Repeated reassurance keeps the loop going; a task ends it.

avoiding: people crowding him when he's stuck on something

triggers.trigger: an object or task that won't work (pump, zipper, lid) and being asked about it
earlySigns: holds the object out to someone
triggers.escalation: destroys the object with his hands, then hits whoever speaks to him next — one blow, no warning, then it's over
whatHelps: take the object from his hand before you speak
give him something heavy to carry
say nothing about the thing for the rest of the day
whatMakesItWorse: 'What happened?' 'Did you brush your teeth?' — any question
standing close in front of him

motifs.cue: hand him the object for the next thing (towel = swim, plate = meal)

people.name: Casey
people.notes: he knocked Casey out once over a toothpaste pump and apologized all summer; they're fine

goals.text: Walt will hand over a stuck object (the 'help' gesture) before gripping it, in 4 of 5 observed frustrations.
Staff will use no yes/no questions to establish facts with Walt; choices are offered as two real objects.

safetyAlerts: Sudden single strike when frustrated with an object and then questioned. Take the object, make statements, don't ask. He's big; don't stand close in front when his grip tightens.
